title: The smaller array (Sn 4.12)
hook: read it: everyone calls their own truth true
tomorrow: so if everyone's arguing, where does the wise one stand?

segments.voice: Yesterday, quarrels, and where the poem says they start: from what is dear. Today the quarrel gets louder, and everybody in it is sure.

Two hundred replies deep under a cooking video. One person: real carbonara never has cream. Another: my grandmother used cream her whole life. A third posts a link. A fourth calls everyone clueless. Nobody is changing anybody's mind, and nobody is leaving. Now step back a long way, into the Buddha's India, and the same thread is running in the town square. Teachers stand in rows, each one certain, each calling the others fools. And someone turns to the Buddha and asks: so which of them is right?
screen: `TWO HUNDRED REPLIES DEEP.` → `EACH ONE CERTAIN.` → `SO WHICH OF THEM IS RIGHT?`

segments.voice: This is the Smaller Array, the twelfth poem in the chapter of eights in the Sutta Nipata. Array, as in troops lined up for battle. The questioner describes the scene. Each teacher, settled in his own view, says: whoever knows this knows the truth; whoever rejects it is incomplete. They argue, and each calls the other a fool. All of them call themselves experts. Which one speaks the truth? The Buddha doesn't pick a winner. He turns the question around. If someone who won't accept another's teaching is a fool, then every one of them is a fool, because every one of them holds his own view. And if holding your own view makes you wise, then nobody in the square is a fool at all. Either way, the name-calling falls apart. Then the line people remember. Truth is one, the poem says; there is no second, and someone who understands it has nothing to quarrel about. So why are there so many truths in the square? Because, the poem says, each one is led by love of his own view. Each calls it true. That's the answer to the cliffhanger. The poem never says which teacher had it right. It looks at the arguing itself: a crowd of people each holding a mirror and calling it a window.
screen: `TEACHERS IN ROWS, LIKE TROOPS.` · `IF HE'S A FOOL, ALL ARE FOOLS.` · `TRUTH IS ONE, NOT TWO.` · `LED BY LOVE OF THEIR OWN VIEW.` · then, large: `EACH CALLS IT TRUE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one opinion you hold firmly, something small enough to be safe. Now, quietly, out loud, say the best single sentence the other side would say for theirs, the way they'd say it, so that they would nod. Then rest with your breath and notice what it's like to have spoken it.
The Smaller Array: Sutta Nipata 4.12, a poem about rows of teachers, each sure, each calling the others fools. The Buddha answers by looking at the arguing, not by crowning a winner.
Keep this one: each calls it true, me included. Twelve poems of the eights, read.

howItsDone: Readers of the Sutta Nipata's chapter of eights often take it a poem at a day, reading it aloud or slowly, and Theravada teachers use its poems on views to talk about holding opinions loosely.

myth: the poem ends by naming the teacher who had it right
it never names one. it looks at the arguing itself: each one led by love of his own view.
the Buddha turns the insult around: if one is a fool, all are
each holds his own view, so by their own rule every one of them is a fool.

fork.setup: two coworkers have argued all week about the right way to run a project, each calling the other's plan amateur. they ask you to settle it. what would the smaller array do first?
options: point out that each is calling their own plan true, and ask what the project needs.
pick the stronger plan; the poem says truth is one, so one of them must be right.
tell them every plan is equally good, so the whole thing is just opinion.
fork.reveal: the Buddha didn't crown a winner or say every view is fine. he showed that each side, by its own rule, was a fool, and that love of one's own view was doing the arguing.

original.note: Pali: truth. In this poem, truth is one, and there is no second.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poem about which school of thought wins.
what it means: the Buddha doesn't crown a winner; he shows that each side calls its own view true and the other a fool, led by love of that view.
what a scholar hears: Sn 4.12 is the Culaviyuha, paired with the Mahaviyuha (4.13); 'viyuha' is an array, like ranks drawn up for battle.
guess: a poem about rows of teachers, each sure he alone is right
a short sermon on how monks should line up for alms
a list of the small rules a new monk must learn first

chat.says: mural war. ava says bold color is the real version, jun says ink wash. both want me on their side
options: don't crown one. each calls theirs true; ask them what the wall needs.
pick the right one fast. truth is one, so one of them has to win.
tell them art is just opinion, so neither of them can be wrong.
chat.meaning: In the Smaller Array the Buddha doesn't name a winner; he shows each side calling its own view true. Mai can look past the sides to the wall.

tie.story: Teachers in the square each called their own view true and the others fools; the Buddha crowned no one.
tie.friend: Mai doesn't have to pick Ava or Jun; she can ask what the wall needs.
tie.you: where are you calling your own view the only true one?

Sutta Nipata.meaning: an early collection of the Buddha's poems and teachings

chapter of eights.meaning: the fourth chapter of the Sutta Nipata, a set of poems

Smaller Array.meaning: Sutta Nipata 4.12: teachers lined up, each sure he's right

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 4.12 (Culaviyuha Sutta, the Smaller Array)

notes: Sn 4.12 paraphrased throughout (no public-domain translation on the validator's list; Fausboll's 1881 SBE 10 version exists for checking). Confirm: the questioner's description (each says whoever knows this knows the truth, whoever rejects it is incomplete; each calls the other a fool); the 'if one is a fool, all are fools' turn; 'truth is one, there is no second' (ekam hi saccam na dutiyam atthi); and 'led by passion for their own view' as the poem's diagnosis.
'Array' as ranks drawn up for battle (viyuha): confirm the gloss is fair for the title.
The 'mirror called a window' image is the script's own, not the poem's.
Story shape: hook is a scene mid-argument; the teach answers 'which of them is right?' by turning the question.

v3 storyline (Mai, day 1 of 14): before graduation, the art club is painting a mural; Ava and a classmate, Jun, each insist their style is the real version. Mai is in the middle. The arc runs to the unveiling (day 1678) and a look back (1680). Ong appears days 1673 and 1679; Ava throughout.
